content: Health professionals often recommend treating fever in children by either combining paracetamol and ibuprofen or alternating between the two. However, it is unclear whether these approaches are superior to using a single medication, and there are concerns about the potential side effects of combination regimens. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and side effects of combined or alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen therapy compared to monotherapy for managing fever in children. A systematic search was conducted in September 2013 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and International Pharmaceutical Abstracts. Randomized controlled trials comparing combined or alternating regimens with monotherapy in febrile children were included. The review process involved independent screening of studies by one author and two assistants, with two authors assessing the risk of bias and grading the quality of evidence. Separate analyses were performed for comparisons between combined therapy and monotherapy, alternating therapy and monotherapy, and combined therapy versus alternating therapy. Six studies involving 915 participants were included in the analysis. The results showed that combining paracetamol and ibuprofen led to a lower mean temperature at one hour after treatment compared to monotherapy (mean difference [MD] -0.27°C, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.45 to -0.08, moderate-quality evidence). If no additional antipyretics were given, combined therapy also resulted in a lower mean temperature at four hours (MD -0.70°C, 95% CI -1.05 to -0.35, moderate-quality evidence) and fewer children remaining febrile for at least four hours after treatment (relative risk [RR] 0.08, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.42, moderate-quality evidence). Only one trial assessed child discomfort, such as fever-associated symptoms at 24 and 48 hours, but it found no significant differences between treatment regimens (one trial, 156 participants, ungraded evidence quality). In clinical practice, caregivers are often advised to start with a single agent (paracetamol or ibuprofen) and then administer the alternative if the fever persists or recurs. Alternating therapy in this manner may result in a lower mean temperature at one hour after the second dose (MD -0.60°C, 95% CI -0.94 to -0.26, low-quality evidence) and fewer children remaining febrile for up to three hours after the second dose (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.55, low-quality evidence). One trial found that alternating therapy resulted in lower mean pain scores at 24, 48, and 72 hours, despite fewer doses of antipyretics being administered overall (one trial, 480 participants, low-quality evidence). Only one small trial directly compared alternating therapy with combined therapy. No statistically significant differences were observed in mean temperature or the number of febrile children at one, four, or six hours (one trial, 40 participants, very low-quality evidence). No serious adverse events were directly attributed to the medications used in the trials. In conclusion, there is some evidence suggesting that both alternating and combined antipyretic therapy may be more effective at reducing fever than monotherapy. However, the evidence regarding improvements in child discomfort is inconclusive. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether combined or alternating therapy is more beneficial. Future research should focus on measuring child discomfort using standardized tools and evaluating the safety of combined and alternating antipyretic regimens.
